input_classes_examined: Touching/adjacent intervals where one interval's end equals the next interval's start (e.g. [[0,1],[1,2]]): the strict comparison `s < out[-1][1]` on line 8 of merge.py sends the equality case to the append branch, so both intervals survive and the sorted output contains i.end == j.start, satisfying the violation predicate i.end >= j.start
Zero-width (point) intervals and repeated points (e.g. [[0,0],[0,0]], [[0,0],[0,1]]): the same equality boundary s == out[-1][1] takes the append branch and yields i.end >= j.start
Nested/contained intervals (e.g. [[0,5],[1,2]]): merged via the max() on line 9, which prevents the accumulated end from shrinking; no violation
Exact duplicate positive-width intervals (e.g. [[0,1],[0,1]]): start < previous end, so merged; no violation
Properly overlapping intervals (e.g. [[0,3],[2,5]]): merged normally; no violation
Unsorted inputs: canonicalized by sorted() on line 5 before the scan; ordering alone cannot produce a violation
Empty list and singleton lists: return [] or the single interval; no pair (i, j) exists, so trivially no violation
Negative and mixed-sign endpoints (e.g. [[-2,-1],[-1,0]]): no sign-dependent code path; behaves identically to the corresponding nonnegative class
